ecd25b44fedb.text: What do we mean by sustainability?

6f2b32862397.text: Sustainability is not a property a product either has or lacks. It describes how ecological, economic, and social systems interact over time. Because these systems are interconnected, sustainability problems are often called "wicked problems": no single correct answer, and no single discipline can solve them [3]. This makes sustainability a matter of systems thinking — a change in one part of a system can have unexpected effects elsewhere — and of resilience, the capacity to adapt while retaining core function, which matters as much as efficiency.

f5c000f776d5.text: The Brundtland definition (1987) — meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs [1] — is simple and communicable, but criticized as anthropocentric. The "three pillars" model (environmental, social, economic) complements it by stressing their interdependence. The UN SDGs [2] turn these ideas into 17 goals for 2030; they are ambitious and criticized for breadth, but they are the common language iGEM teams use, so we adopt them while staying aware of their limits.

09737bb7b8c5.text: AeroSense is an AI-driven, biologically inspired VOC (volatile organic compound) sensing platform: a living olfactory-receptor layer, custom lock-in optoelectronic hardware, and a neuromorphic classifier modeled on the fly brain, packaged as a portable, cartridge-based electronic nose. We work on two layers and keep them separate throughout this page:

dbc2f72cc1a5.text: Application theme — stored food (Food & Nutrition track). Mold- and pathogen-VOC screening in stored tea, coffee, and other dried foods. Our public survey and most of our education work belong here.

479eedca9588.text: Commercial beachhead — fruit export supply chain. Early detection of fungal disease and ripeness in Taiwan's banana and mango exports, with tea processing as the second-stage expansion. Its buyers are institutions (exporters, packing houses, associations) rather than individual consumers, which is why we entered here first.

cae630ae3e01.text: We asked not only whether the technology could work, but whether it should, for whom, and at what cost to which other goal. Our Human Practices engagement shaped the answers: the Taoyuan District Agricultural Improvement Station's Plant Protection Lab, the Taiwan Banana Research Institute, farmers' associations and facility farms, an electronic-nose company's Chief Science Officer, Chia-Nien Biotechnology, an analytical-instrumentation (GC-MS/LC-MS) professional, a patent attorney, our academic advisors, and the pupils, students, and peer teams we taught and learned from.

9552533303b7.text: We anchor this page on four goals our work has actually touched — SDG 2, 9, 12, and 17 — with SDG 3, 4, and 10 as supporting connections. We are at a preliminary stage: no full life-cycle assessment, cost analysis, or market study yet, and hardware validation is still in progress. This page is therefore critical reflection, not a promise.

5a79af12abf7.text: Target 2.4 — Resilient agricultural practices. Informed by our field interviews [6], we estimate fungal-disease-related risk in Taiwan's banana and mango export sector at roughly NT$3.51 billion/year (about 33.6% of NT$10.445 billion annual output value). Today's detection is either visual sampling — by which point infection has often spread — or slow, destructive lab assays that cannot cover a whole shipment. Flagging a VOC signal before symptoms appear lets exporters, packing houses, and cooperatives isolate, reroute, or re-time a batch instead of losing it. Globally, roughly 14% of food is lost between harvest and retail [4], so the supply-chain link we target is a known weak point, not a niche one.

So far we have interviewed only agricultural institutions upstream of them.]Next step: interview at least one exporter or packing house, and measure detection lead time against visual symptom onset in validation.

27e77730fa77.text: Target 2.3 — Productivity and incomes of small-scale producers. This is the tension we have to be honest about. The instrumentation professional we interviewed [9] expected low willingness to pay among individual farmers, and a device sold directly to smallholders would add cost without adding income. Selling to associations and cooperatives lets a smallholder's income protection come from a shared, institution-level tool they do not have to buy or fear — but this is a design intention, not a validated outcome. Next step: a cost model that shows who pays, who benefits, and whether the benefit reaches smallholders.

4b1023e0db79.text: AeroSense integrates biological sensing, custom optoelectronics, and neuromorphic AI into a field-deployable platform built on the team's own peer-reviewed research.

e8017b40246b.text: Target 9.5 — Research and technological capability. The e-nose CSO told us the industry bottleneck is the sensing element — selectivity, sensitivity, lifetime, reproducibility [7]. AeroSense responds with a living, self-renewing receptor (Drosophila OR/Orco with the GCaMP6 reporter in a standard mammalian cell line), structurally different from a static chemical film. Our classifier is modeled on the fly mushroom body's PN–KC–MBON circuit and has a direct published lineage through our advisors' Science Advances paper [10], which is open access (CC BY 4.0), with code on Dryad and data on Zenodo.

62c6d581ebd2.text: Target 9.b — Domestic technology development. Our first readout used a blue LED and a camera (CMOS, 30 frames per second). It worked on the bench, but outside the lab ambient light and sensor noise swamped a faint cell signal, which is what the e-nose industry had warned us about. We replaced it with an in-house design: four LEDs, each modulated at its own frequency, excite four wells that share one photodiode, and an ESP32 runs digital lock-in detection to read each channel while rejecting room light and slow drift. We state its limits as plainly. Excitation light that leaks onto the detector at the same frequency as the signal survives lock-in, and because the wells share one detector and a gas space, physical mixing between wells still needs calibration, so emission filtering, blank wells, and per-well calibration are still required. The housing and circuit board exist only as CAD and layout, with fabrication and full assembly pending, so we have not yet measured the platform's power draw or noise performance, and we do not yet know its net footprint against the biological layer (culture media, consumables, cold chain). Validation is planned in five stages — component bench tests, electronics-only lock-in, fluorescent-dye calibration, environmental-noise robustness, live-cell end-to-end — and is not complete. Next step: fabricate and assemble the board, then report measured noise rejection, crosstalk, and power at each stage as it completes.

cadd442b9a6a.text: Non-destructive, reusable-cartridge screening reduces the produce, reagents, and consumables wasted by destructive testing, and prevents good produce from being discarded on suspicion alone.

1d1e5890f101.text: Target 12.3 — Food loss. Spoilage often means discarding a whole batch once contamination is visible, days after the VOC signal first appeared. At the household end of the stored-food theme, our public survey [5] points to a related problem. Most respondents (78%) understood that removing visible mold does not always make food safe, but only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk, with 27% unsure and 15% holding the misconception. People who judge by sight and smell will either throw away food that may be fine or keep food that is not. A tool that can say "this portion is still fine" cuts needless waste just as flagging real risk cuts unsafe consumption; we treat both as one design problem, hence risk tiers. We have not measured how much food households or businesses actually discard, and the survey is self-reported by people who chose to respond, so it shows where to look rather than how common each belief is. Next step: add the perspective of shops and warehouses, and test the tier output with real users.

b339224654bc.text: Target 12.5 — Waste prevention and reuse. Destructive assays (PCR, ELISA, GC-MS sample prep) consume the sample and generate single-use chemical waste per test. Our cartridge is designed to be non-destructive and reusable across multiple readings. A self-renewing cell population should need replacing less often than conventional e-nose sensors, some of which the industry says need near-daily replacement — but we have not validated this, and we claim no net environmental benefit until we have. Next step: a cartridge lifetime test, then a simple screening LCA against a destructive-assay baseline; recyclable or biodegradable housing to be evaluated.

27cb1d64d039.text: Target 12.4 — Chemicals and waste over the life cycle. We have not yet quantified our own wet-lab footprint (reagents, culture consumables, single-use plastics). Previous iGEM teams have published such self-audits, and we will follow them: classify reagents by hazard, quantify plastic and consumable waste, and identify where segregation or reuse is possible. [Insert audit figures once collected — e.g. approximate plastic waste in kg, reagents by hazard class, existing reuse practices.]Next step: complete the audit before the wiki freeze.

c00a63a8f57a.text: SDG 3 — Good Health and Well-being. A detected VOC signal is not a food-safety verdict [8], so AeroSense is a screening tool that recommends confirmatory testing, never a diagnostic replacement. The risk-tier output is the design response. A possible medical direction, raised in early discussions with the S.Y.Dao Cancer Prevention Foundation, is only exploratory: it would bring regulatory demands that our current agricultural and food screening does not face.

feee0d870183.text: SDG 4 — Quality Education. Our education work targets the specific misunderstanding the survey found, not a general warning that mold is dangerous. It includes a free online learning platform of five short modules, a science camp for upper-grade pupils at a rural elementary school, a university workshop, and a reusable teacher toolkit so that others can run the same sessions without us. We do not yet have completed learning-outcome data, and we will report results as measured.

0ae62b353d06.text: SDG 10 — Reduced Inequalities. The farmer-adoption-resistance finding is also an inequality risk: an individual-farmer product would likely reach only well-resourced buyers. Targeting associations and cooperatives is our current response — not yet a validated equitable outcome.

43a58927a545.text: Our own waste (SDG 12). Living-cell cartridges are themselves a consumable. Lower replacement frequency is our hypothesis; only the LCA can confirm a net benefit.

4accd980b606.text: Who benefits from innovation (SDG 9 vs. SDG 2/10). Patents are necessary for commercial defensibility, and we are preparing a filing through our university. But restrictive licensing could limit affordability and decide whether exporters or smallholder-serving associations get access.

7dd7b2b2ccf9.text: Open science vs. patent timing. Our patent attorney advised that our own early disclosure can later count against novelty, so we are holding back some technical detail until a filing is made. This sits uneasily with iGEM's open-science norms and with our wish to leave reusable work for future teams. We resolve it by sequencing — file first, then publish — and by keeping our education materials fully open, because they do not depend on that detail.

9a253335124a.text: Partnership maturity (SDG 17). Presenting every interview as a partnership would overstate how far our validation has gone; hence the maturity table above.

def0863cd12a.text: Resilience vs. equity (SDG 2). A tool that makes exporters more resilient can still fail smallholders if the economics do not flow downstream. We do not assume the two move together.

acc7c7e2b7c6.text: Only the measurements that decide whether the sustainability claims above hold. Everything else is in the Engineering and Human Practices pages.

5fcac58e0e30.text: Social. Priority beneficiaries are smallholder farmers and the cooperatives that serve them. The plan is to keep the institution-level buyer model, keep the tool a screening aid rather than a verdict, and use plain-language risk tiers so that farmers and households can act on the result. On the education side, we leave free, reusable materials so that teachers and other teams can run the same sessions without us.

df1360454022.text: Economic. Earlier detection targets a sector-level risk of about NT$3.51 billion/year. Before claiming savings, we need the exporter/packing-house interview and a cost model. Commercial staging follows our Entrepreneurship page: banana and mango first, tea second.

6bf32ef24769.text: Environmental. The aim is less food discarded and less single-use assay waste. The claim is conditional on the LCA and lifetime test, which will show whether a living-cell cartridge is a net gain.

5379d776e4ac.text: For future teams. We document the open items above so that next season's team, or another team, can pick them up directly.

1a11f997ee22.text: AeroSense advances agricultural resilience, technological capability, and cross-sector partnership in some respects, and leaves open questions for others: its own cartridge waste, who benefits from patented innovation, how open science and patent timing fit together, and whether resilience reaches smallholders. We have named these trade-offs, tied each to a metric and a next step, and kept a clear line between what is validated and what is intended.
